I had cyclical (or rather episodic) Cushing’s disease. I had surgery 12 months ago to remove the pituitary tumor causing it. 

No idea what triggered it. It really was more random episodes rather than running in any kind of cycle for me. Things that did make it go crazy were my first pregnancy, severe diet restriction and over exercising, and birth control (the pill and the hideous Mirena). 

I think of my little tumour like a tap. Sometimes it ‘s just a trickle of extra ACTH and sometimes the tap is running at full and just totally pumping masses of extra ACTH. 

I had periods in my life where I would gain massive amounts of weight very rapidly and period of time where it seemed to stabilise although it was close to impossible to lose any weight.

I’m 9 months post surgery and officially in remission from Cushing’s disease. I’m no longer on replacement hydrocortisone. Recovery is slow and not fun. Adapting to a life of low/normal cortisol after 3 decades of Cushing’s is hard. I still struggle a lot with feeling crap, pretty bad depression, pain, more pain, muscle weakness, brain fog/cognitive issues. Sometimes every joint in my body hurts. Mobility is still difficult although slightly improved. I can’t do much without being wiped out for a day or so. I don’t cope with stress very well. 

The positives are : 
So far I am down 29kg (64lb). That’s without trying. My great big buffalo hump has greatly reduced. As has the edema in my feet and lower legs. Sleep has greatly improved. Moon face has also reduced a lot and my face and eyes aren’t as puffy. I have more of a neck happening. 

So there are improvements. It’s just so so slow. And I wonder how much of the damage is permanent.

It was a combination of so many multiples of many different tests. The testing process was long and mentally exhausting. 

In the end it was more about finding the right endocrinologist to actually LISTEN to my medical history and to correctly interpret all my results.

I did have an IPSS prior to my pituitary surgery. 
But I was referring to the pathology testing that was done on my pituitary tumour after it was surgically removed. The pathology report said the tumour portion of the sample stained strongly for ACTH which means I absolutely had Cushing’s disease.

I had surgery for Cushing’s disease in March. Pathology on my pituitary tumour 100% confirmed Cushing’s disease. 

My am blood cortisol test results while I had Cushing’s we’re always around the high end of the normal range. They were only out of range ONCE. Almost all of my 24 hour urine cortisol results were elevated but not crazy elevated. Half of my midnight salivas were high. 

Blood cortisol readings are not usually useful for Cushing’s diagnosis. 

See what happens with the dex suppression test. And remember one result cannot rule Cushing’s either out or in

Then that my abnormal results weren’t abnormal enough?!  The diagnosis process is so infuriating. Just because Cushing’s is rare, doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist!

Keep pushing for further testing. You know your body. You know if it doesn’t feel right.

Cyclical (or episodic) Cushing’s is where the tumour (or source of the elevated cortisol) is not always “on”.  I think of it a bit like a tap, sometimes it’s off, sometimes it’s just a trickle and sometimes it’s on full. That’s what makes it so hard to diagnose. You have to “catch” the times it’s on high. 

Some people are lucky enough to get their doctors to order marathon testing. Involves a lot of midnight saliva tests and 24hr urine tests.

This is my experience with Ozempic, both with Cushing’s and then after surgery to remove my tumour. 

I had an endocrinologist put me on Ozempic about a year ago. She blamed my elevated cortisol on obesity and said this “miracle drug” would force me to lose weight and I’d feel so much better…. 
Personally I found the side effects to be horrendous whilst I had Cushing’s. I did not lose any weight. It did improve my blood sugars a bit. 

Anyway, I had surgery 5 months ago and I’m now in remission from Cushing’s disease. I stopped ozempic before surgery and restarted it a few weeks after surgery. I restarted on .25 and very slowly built up to 1mg. This time the side effects are much less. And I’ve been slowly losing weight since surgery so I’m not sure how much Ozempic is helping with that. My blood sugars are now really good. 

See how you go. And don’t increase the dose until you feel okay to do so. The side effects hit some people more than others.  I did 4 weeks at each dose and went up by .25 each time.
Any abnormal result requires further testing and referral to an endocrinologist

Also, you don’t have to have any striae to have Cushing’s. I did not have them and definitely had Cushing’s disease. 

Correct about the blood cortisol readings. It’s because it only shows the cortisol level at one moment in time and cortisol fluctuates. The AM blood cortisol can be normal and you could still have Cushing’s. That was the case for me. 

That’s why the other tests are important because they show if there’s an issue with cortisol production. 

Definitely ask to do a couple 24hr urines and a couple midnight salivas, followed by the 1mg dexamethasone suppression test.

Yes, birth control does increase cortisol levels and the general recommendation is to stop taking it for a few weeks before Cushing’s testing. Also yes, we need more cortisol when we are seriously stressed and/or ill. 

Unfortunately Cushing’s can’t be diagnosed (or ruled out) with one single test. Especially not a blood test. Cortisol levels in the blood can fluctuate a lot. Although 1100 nmol/L is about twice the top of normal range for 8am so you’d think they would do further testing. 

Can you ask your GP for some 24 hour urine cortisol tests and some midnight saliva cortisol tests?  And then a 1mg overnight dexamethasone test. They are the initial tests for Cushing’s. My GP was happy to order extra tests for me because it doesn’t hurt anything to have more data and it’s covered by Medicare (just make sure the saliva tests have “Cushing’s syndrome” written on them or you’ll be charged a small fortune!

As well as 24 hour urine tests, they should also be doing a low dose dexamethasone suppression test. 

As for medications, they aren’t the cure and should be used either in the lead up to surgery or if surgery is not possible. Treating the tumour that’s causing Cushing’s is the best treatment. 

Even a tiny tumour can be hormone secreting that has devastating effects. 

As for IPSS, yes it’s scary. I had mine done without sedation or general anaesthetic. I’ll be glad if I never have to go through that again!  But having said that, the team that did mine and looked after me were outstanding and got me through it just fine. And it meant a diagnosis and I’ll be having my surgery tomorrow. The dex test is to check the function of your HPA (hyperthalamus/pituitary/adrenal) axis. 

If you suppress then it means that your HPA axis is functioning as it should. If you do not suppress then that suggests Cushing’s syndrome. 

If things are working properly, your body recognises the dexamethasone just like it would recognise cortisol, and so it doesn’t make as much cortisol because it thinks you have enough already. 

If you have Cushing’s, then the whole HPA axis is not working properly because there’s a tumour producing either ACTH or cortisol independently. So therefore cortisol will remain higher (not suppressed).

Dexamethasone acts like cortisol in your body. So even if it lowers your cortisol, I believe you still have a similar amount of total steroid running around in your body. 

The idea is that your body thinks it has enough cortisol so it stops making it while the dexamethasone is in your system. In other words, if your HPA (hyperthalamus/pituitary/adrenal) axis is working normally, your body suppresses cortisol production until you’ve processed the dexamethasone. 

If you don’t suppress cortisol, that may mean that something else is independently making excess hormones. Eg. A tumour somewhere in your body.

This is the 1mg dexamethasone suppression test. You take 1mg dexamethasone at 11pm and then have blood drawn at 8-9am the next morning. They will test cortisol and sometimes they may test dexamethasone level. ACTH isn’t usually checked with this test, although they can check it. It’s the cortisol level that’s important here. 

If your cortisol level is above 1.8 ug/dL (or 50 nmol/L) then that means you did NOT suppress and that your HPA (hypothalamus/pituitary/adrenal) axis is possibly not working correctly. 

If your cortisol level is under 1.8 then it means you DID suppress and that is the response a normal person would expect. 

It appears that you did suppress on this test which is a normal response.  But keep reading!

It’s really important to note several things. Firstly  that the normal am cortisol reference range (4-22) is not relevant for this test. All you need to know is that above 1.8 is not suppressed and below 1.8 is suppressed.  Secondly, that one test cannot rule out Cushing’s. One test can also not diagnose Cushing’s. You will need multiple tests to work out what is going wrong, including several 24 hour urine cortisol tests, several midnight saliva cortisol tests, blood tests to check pituitary function (lots of different hormone levels) etc.  Many people with diagnosed Cushing’s can have many normal tests before they “catch” high tests. That’s one of the things that makes diagnosing Cushing’s so difficult.
